name: Bespoke suit

lead: A bespoke suit is made from a pattern drafted individually for the wearer, rather than adjusted from a standard size. The appearance payoff is fit: shoulders, chest, sleeves and waist follow the actual body, which can make a frame look more balanced and a build look more deliberate.

It is a service rather than a product. The tailor takes many measurements, cuts and bastes the cloth, and usually holds two or three fittings before finishing. Lifters on the T Nation forum describe it as one answer to the problem of big chests, thighs and shoulders that off-the-rack sizes do not fit.

paras: People choose fabric and style in a consultation, are measured, and return for fittings while the garment is built; the full process commonly takes two to three months. Some train-and-tailor forum members buy off-the-rack and have it altered, use made-to-measure, or commission one or two bespoke suits for work.

The main drawbacks are cost, time and the need for repeat fittings. A body that changes size after the pattern is made, for example during muscle gain or fat loss, can affect fit. The term 'bespoke' is not tightly regulated: in 2008 the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that calling a partly machine-made suit bespoke was not misleading.

angle.text: A bespoke suit removes the compromise between chest and waist size that standard patterns impose, which lifters on forums describe as the reason they commission or alter suits. The fit is visible immediately when worn.

lead: A bespoke suit is a suit made to an individual's specifications from a pattern drafted from scratch, as opposed to made-to-measure, which alters a standard-size pattern [1]. The word comes from 'bespeak', meaning to order something to be made, and is associated with Savile Row in London [1].

Its use for appearance is about fit. Because the pattern is built on the wearer's own measurements, the garment follows the shoulders and posture rather than approximating them [1]. T Nation members, many of them lifters with broad chests and shoulders but narrower waists, describe the problem of off-the-rack jackets either fitting the chest and leaving the waist loose, or the reverse [2][3].
The topic is documented mainly through general reference sources and forum discussion; no studies have examined how tailoring affects how a person is perceived.

paras: In a bespoke commission, the customer chooses fabric and styling at a consultation, the tailor takes often twenty or more measurements and drafts a pattern, then cuts and bastes the cloth. Two or three fittings usually follow before the suit is finished, and the process commonly takes two to three months [1].

Made-to-measure alters an existing standard pattern, and is faster and generally cheaper. Newer digital patterning and lean workshop methods can produce bespoke garments faster and at prices closer to made-to-measure [1].

Training-focused forums raise the problem of building a physique that standard sizing does not cover. In one T Nation thread about where big men buy clothes, replies note that the problem is mostly suits, jackets and dress shirts, and that the usual advice is to find a tailor [2]. Another poster recommends made-to-measure shirts for people who cannot close the top button [4].

One member in a thread on tailored jackets says that sizing up for the chest leaves sleeves too long and the waist like a circus tent, and that they invested in two bespoke suits for work while buying others online [5]. Others buy second-hand and rely on a tailor for adjustment [6]. Posters also mention bespoke as a status marker in the more boastful posts of the forum [7].

In 2008 the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that describing a partly machine-made suit as bespoke was not misleading. The Savile Row Bespoke Association disagreed with the ruling but did not formally challenge it [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation, tailoring comes up mainly in threads by lifters whose builds do not fit standard sizes [2][5].
